analysis.one_liner: Lets people exposed to toxic PFAS chemicals sue manufacturers and get polluter-paid medical monitoring.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2024 with three cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and never received a markup or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create, for the first time, a federal lawsuit right for people who were significantly exposed to PFAS — the long-lasting 'forever chemicals' used in manufacturing that CDC has found in Americans' blood. Exposed individuals or class-action groups could sue companies that made the chemicals, and courts could order those companies to pay for ongoing medical checkups to catch PFAS-related diseases early. The bill also lets courts loosen the usual scientific-proof standard when there is not enough toxicology data, and order companies to fund new health studies of their own chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits: People significantly exposed to PFAS — the bill's own findings cite studies detecting PFAS in the drinking water of at least 200 million Americans [S2]. Today there is no federal statutory cause of action for PFAS harm, so exposed people must rely on patchwork state laws [S2]. The bill would let them sue in any federal district court, gives them a presumption of significant exposure if the chemical maker released PFAS in their area for a year or if PFAS shows up in their blood, and shifts the cost of medical monitoring exams and rebuttal testing onto the companies responsible [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting significantly exposed individuals or classes sue PFAS makers in any U.S. district court for legal and equitable relief [S2].
Codifies a medical monitoring remedy: courts can award periodic diagnostic exams when exposure raises the risk of PFAS-linked disease, shifting those costs from patients to responsible parties [S2].

Sets a rebuttable presumption of significant exposure when a defendant's PFAS was released where the person lived for at least a year, or when testing detects PFAS in the person's blood — and makes the defendant pay for any rebuttal testing [S2].

Allows courts to lower the scientific-proof standard for proving increased disease risk when toxicological data is lacking, and to order defendants to fund new epidemiological or toxicological studies of their chemicals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that manufactured PFAS or used it in manufacturing and should have foreseen human exposure. They would face federal lawsuits including class actions, bear the cost of medical monitoring awards, and pay for independent rebuttal testing and court-ordered health studies [S2]. Some of these costs could ultimately show up in product prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill loosens the usual evidentiary bar: when toxicology data is insufficient, courts may lower the standard of scientific proof for showing increased disease risk until better data exists [S2]. A reasonable objection is that this invites large class actions against companies whose specific chemicals are not yet proven harmful, with settlement costs passed on to consumers in prices.

The presumption of exposure can be triggered by one year of presence in an area where a defendant's PFAS was released, or by any detection of PFAS in blood, which is now nearly universal in Americans [S2]. Critics would argue this makes it hard to tie a specific defendant to a specific individual's exposure, encouraging broad litigation rather than pinpointed accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living with PFAS exposure and elevated disease risk, the benefit is concrete: a federal right to sue and polluter-funded medical monitoring that could catch cancers and other diseases earlier [S2]. The main cost falls on chemical manufacturers, and some of it may be passed to consumers through prices; the lowered proof standard could also produce sprawling litigation where a defendant's link to a particular harm is thin. On balance, the bill is designed to move exposure costs from victims to the companies that created the chemicals, which is the standard tort rationale — but its breadth would be tested heavily in court.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees and to an environment subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania introduced the PFAS Accountability Act of 2024 on February 1, 2024, joined by Reps. Jerrold Nadler and Dan Kildee [S1][S2].
The bill was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee [S4].
On February 2, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials — the last action ever taken on it [S4].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

The bill's findings state that, before enactment, no federal statutory cause of action existed for people harmed by long-term PFAS exposure, and cite studies finding PFAS in the drinking water of at least 200 million Americans [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that made or used PFAS are better off: because no committee ever took up the bill, they avoided a new federal litigation channel, a medical-monitoring cost obligation, and court-ordered funding of health studies of their own chemicals.

for.name: Madeleine Dean
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Jerrold Nadler and Dan Kildee
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill as its only other original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and its Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials Subcommittee; never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never took it up for a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were House Democrats (Dean plus three cosponsors out of 216), no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run House committees never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would expose companies that made or used PFAS to federal lawsuits and class actions, mandatory medical monitoring awards, and court-ordered funding of health studies. The bill died in committee, so that liability never materialized. [S2][S4]

industries.industry: Independent medical testing and toxicology providers
industries.note: Under the bill, defendants would pay for court-appointed independent testing and any court-ordered epidemiological or toxicological studies, creating paid work for testing labs and research firms. The bill's death leaves this potential market unrealized. [S2]
